w: Prime Minister Rainilaiarivony ran the Kingdom of Madagascar from this hilltop palace through the late 1800s; today it's a museum holding roughly 1,466 objects of royal history salvaged from the devastating 1995 fire at the nearby Rova. Everything here survived only because someone ran into the flames to save it.
s: Rescued treasures from the Rova's 1995 fire
_facts: Residence of Prime Minister Rainilaiarivony, who governed the Kingdom of Madagascar in the late 19th century
Located on the highest hilltop of Antananarivo
Now a museum housing an estimated 1,466 objects of historical importance rescued from the 1995 fire at the Rova of Antananarivo

w: Set in Andohalo, the upper town where the city looks down on itself, this cathedral has served as the seat of the Archdiocese of Antananarivo since it went up - its facade turned deliberately west, facing straight down into the heart of the capital it was built to watch over.
s: The Catholic seat above old Andohalo
_facts: Catholic cathedral in the Andohalo area of the upper town (haute ville), Antananarivo
Seat of the Archdiocese of Antananarivo
Facade faces the city centre to the west

n: Botanical and Zoological Garden of Tsimbazaza
w: Behind the zoo enclosures sits a stranger collection: the skeleton of an extinct elephant bird, alongside pygmy hippos and giant lemurs that no longer walk Madagascar at all. Add the country's largest herbarium, some 80,000 specimens strong, and this one park holds a museum's worth of a vanished Madagascar.
s: Elephant birds and giant lemurs, in one park
_facts: Zoo and botanical garden in the Tsimbazaza neighbourhood of Antananarivo, said to house the finest collection of Malagasy wildlife
Museum holds tribal carvings and skeletons of extinct megavertebrates, including an elephant bird, pygmy hippos and giant lemurs
Contains Madagascar's largest herbarium, with roughly 80,000 plant specimens
